sourcing_rule: Every scored item requires >=2 independent existing published sources to agree on the fact. No fresh human/expert annotation was performed. Items where sources disagreed or only one source existed were dropped from scoring and logged in dropped_items instead.
answer_format_rule: Question is open natural language. Model must end its response with a line 'Final answer: <value>', scored by exact/normalized string match against expected_answer or answer_aliases. No LLM judge.

dropped_items.reason: Sources disagree substantially: ~132 BPM vs ~170 BPM, not an octave-doubling relationship (unlike Let It Be's cleanly-explained split), so no confident single value could be assigned without a human listening to resolve it. Dropped per the no-agreement-no-item rule rather than guessed.

Song swapped out of the pilot entirely: 'Autumn Leaves' is a jazz standard performed in different keys by different artists (Bb major/G minor OR G major/E minor depending on the recording/fake book), so 'what key is this song in' is not well-defined without anchoring to one specific named recording. Replaced with 'Take Five', which has one canonical, unambiguous recording.

Dropped during the 2026-08-16 second-source pass, not before it. The original single-source claim (i-iv-VI-VII, F#m-Bm-D-E) came from an aggregated search summary. Attempting to find a second source instead surfaced a direct contradiction: Hooktheory-based analysis describes the verse as an F#m-G#m-A Dorian loop, a materially different progression. Rather than pick a winner ourselves (which would be exactly the kind of unverified call the no-human-annotator rule rules out), the item is dropped. This is the clearest demonstration in the pilot of the citation-gate rule doing its job -- it caught a wrong fact that had already been written into the file, not just an unconfirmed one.

known_limitations: A second-source pass (2026-08-16) resolved most of the originally single-sourced items: 24 of 27 remaining items now meet the >=2-independent-source bar. In the process it also caught one item (billie_jean_progression) whose original single source was flatly wrong, not just unconfirmed -- moved to dropped_items rather than corrected by guesswork.

3 items remain single-sourced after the second pass and are still flagged rather than trusted: let_it_be_genre, billie_jean_genre, billie_jean_bridge_device. All three failed a real retry attempt, not just an unattempted one -- the second-source search either found nothing specific enough (bridge pedal tone) or found only a loosely-related corroboration (album-level vs. song-level genre tags).

Automatic BPM/key-detection sites (SongBPM, Tunebat, GetSongKey, etc.) were treated with caution, not as independent sources of each other, since they likely share correlated failure modes (e.g. the same octave-doubling error appeared across multiple such sites for both Let It Be and Take Five). Where possible, a non-algorithmic source (published sheet music tempo marking, Wikipedia prose, an accredited course handout) was preferred as at least one of the two required sources.
Genre labels are treated as lower-confidence throughout -- they are inherently somewhat subjective editorial judgments, not objective facts in the same sense as a key signature or personnel credit.

This entire sourcing pass was done via automated web search/fetch in one sitting, not by a human researcher -- it should be read as a demonstration of the citation-gate mechanism working (including catching its own earlier mistake), not as a fully audited final ground-truth set. A human spot-check before this is used for real scoring would still be worthwhile.
